lesson.title: Two Names, One List: List Aliasing
lesson.summary: Because lists are mutable, assigning one variable to another does not copy the list, it creates a second name pointing at the exact same list object, so a change made through either name is visible through both.
lesson.body:
Earlier in this unit you saw list mutability, the fact that a list's contents can change after it is created, and you have used ordinary variable assignment countless times for numbers and strings. List aliasing is what happens when those two ideas meet: because a list is mutable and a variable is just a name bound to an object, writing alias = original does not create a second list. It creates a second name that refers to the very same list object as original.

```python
original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original
alias.append(4)
print(original)
print(alias)
```

This prints [1, 2, 3, 4] twice. Appending 4 through alias changed the one and only list both names point to, so original sees the change too, even though the code never mentioned original on that line. This is not a bug or a special case, it is simply what assignment means for any mutable object in Python, and it is the exact same mechanism behind the list-repetition trap you may have already seen, where [row] * 3 filled a grid with three names for one shared row.

If you actually want an independent second list, one that starts out equal but can change separately, you need to make a real copy rather than an alias. There are a few equivalent ways to do this: original[:], a full slice; original.copy(); or list(original). All three build a new list object with the same elements.

```python
original = [1, 2, 3]
copy = original[:]
copy.append(4)
print(original)
print(copy)
```

This prints [1, 2, 3], unchanged, then [1, 2, 3, 4]. Because copy is a distinct list object, mutating it leaves original alone. Note carefully that this kind of copy is shallow: it copies the outer list's references, so if your list contains other mutable objects, like lists inside a list, those inner objects are still shared between the original and the copy. The core habit to build from this concept is to pause, whenever you write name2 = name1 with a list, and ask yourself honestly whether you wanted a second name for the same list, which is aliasing, or a genuinely separate list, which requires an explicit copy. This distinction becomes even more precise once you look at identity versus equality next.
